judge_assessment.explanation: The mathematics is exactly as the judge describes - I recomputed A' = (6,3); B'C' = 7.5 and A'C' = 12.5 for the sail; k = 21/6 = 3.5 with width 14; Q' = (1+3(3-1), 2+3(5-2)) = (7,11); 24 by 36 with area factor 2.4^2 = 5.76; DE = 6, D'E' = 12, quotient 2; 0.72/144 = 0.005 and 4.8/12 = 0.4; and K'L' = 6 for the doubled triangle. Problem 8 is correctly flagged manual with a good descriptor. The judge's "eight readable dilation applications" is true, but its implicit claim that verification is complete is not: problem 7 opens with "Explain what Ben did wrong" - a named-error diagnosis that the problem grades - and verify.json id 7 carries only two `eval` entries with no `manual`, so final_response.md's statement that "One item is flagged for manual review, correctly" undercounts by at least one. Problem 6(c) has the same shape on a smaller scale: "say what that quotient is" (it is the scale factor) is a written response covered by nothing but the numeric 2.

strengths_to_preserve: Problem 7 is the best-designed item on the sheet: the planted value 0.06 is declared as a trap with the exact misconception ("divided the area by the scale factor instead of by its square"), so the key's Common wrong answers block converts a wrong area into a diagnosis of the k-versus-k^2 confusion.

The sheet separates origin-centred from centre-based dilations as distinct printed rules - problem 1 uses (x,y) -> (kx,ky) and problem 4 uses h + k(x-h) on the map pin P(1,2) - instead of letting the shortcut stand in for the definition.

Units are stated in every stem and carried through: the model-car item mixes metres and square metres in one problem (0.4 m and 0.005 m^2) so the length-versus-area scaling has to be decided, not guessed.

Problem 8's manual entry names the two things the drawing must show - the three vertex lines concurrent at the centre, and similarity argued from the dilation rather than measured - which makes an open construction gradeable.

root_causes.description: A misconception-analysis item was recorded as fully machine-verified because its numeric repair is checkable, leaving the explanation (which the stem asks for first) outside the manual-review set.
evidence: worksheet.tex problem 7 asks "Explain what Ben did wrong, then give the correct area ... and the model's length"; verify.json id 7 has two `eval` entries (0.005 and 0.4) and no `manual` entry.
verify.json contains exactly one `manual` entry, for problem 8; final_response.md line 43 states that one item is flagged "correctly".
Problem 6(c) "Divide the image length by the pre-image length and say what that quotient is" is likewise covered only by the numeric entry m/n -> 2.

root_causes.description: Each problem prints a single "Answer: ____" even when the stem asks for three separate things, because the guidance is one answer location per problem rather than per requested value.
evidence: worksheet.tex problem 7 asks for an explanation, an area and a length and prints one auto-emitted answer blank.
Problem 5 asks for two side lengths and an area ratio (24, 36, 5.76) and prints one blank; problem 3 asks for the scale factor and the width and prints one.

improvements.title: Record every explanation, diagnosis and named-error item as a manual entry
improvements.proposed_change: Treat an item that asks the student to explain, justify, describe, name the wrong move, or draw/mark a representation as a MANUAL response even when a numeric part of the same problem is machine-checkable. SKILL.md and references/manual-review-aid.md should state the rule, and the response-coverage gate should scan each problem segment for imperative prose asks (Explain, Describe, Say why, Which ... did, State how, Sketch, Draw and label) and fail when the problem carries no `manual` entry. Here problem 7's "Explain what Ben did wrong" must force a `manual` entry alongside its two `eval` entries.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture worksheet with a problem stem containing "Explain what went wrong" and a verify id holding only `eval` entries must make the gate exit non-zero; adding a `manual` entry for that problem must make it exit 0. The fixture passes every gate today, so the test fails before the fix and passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: The manual-review list delivered in final_response.md becomes true, and graders stop treating an unreviewed explanation as machine-verified.
improvements.risk: Keyword scanning will flag scaffolding prose that is not a graded ask ("Explain to yourself why..."), so the rule needs an explicit opt-out and a short allowlist to avoid pushing authors toward manual-everything.

improvements.title: One answer blank per requested value - no lumped blank, no orphan blank
improvements.proposed_change: SKILL.md's "Answer location (every problem gets one)" should read "every REQUESTED VALUE gets one": a multi-part problem ends each part with its own \ansline/\answerline inside the stem (which already suppresses \problem's automatic blank, as the preamble documents), and no problem emits a trailing unlabelled blank once every part already has one. Extend tests/check_answer_line.py, which today only binds units, to compare answer-location macros against the distinct non-manual verify entries for the problem id and fail in both directions. Here problems 3, 5 and 7 each need one blank per requested value (2, 3 and 3 respectively) instead of the single auto-emitted line.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture pair for tests/check_answer_line.py: (a) a problem printing one \ansline against four verify entries must exit non-zero, and (b) the same problem with one \ansline per part must exit 0; plus (c) a problem whose parts all carry blanks and which then emits a trailing \ansline must exit non-zero. All three pass today because the checker never counts blanks.
improvements.expected_impact: The student knows where each requested value goes and the grader can map a Quick Answers row onto the sheet position by position.
improvements.risk: Per-part blanks consume vertical space, so a few dense sheets will gain a page; the gate must also allow a deliberate \noansline on sketch/proof items.

case_summary: A polished dilation workshop: eight genuinely applied problems, correct coordinates, lengths, areas and scale factors throughout, a well-declared k-versus-k^2 trap, and a manual descriptor on problem 8 that makes an open construction gradeable. The defect is the verification label, not the mathematics: problem 7 asks the student to diagnose Ben's error in words and is nevertheless recorded as fully machine-verified, so the delivered manual-review list is short by one and a graded written response reaches the student with nobody assigned to read it.
